turn_text: Senator, with regard to this appropriations process, if it is the intent of the majority and of the leadership to use policy riders to defund particular areas, there is the winning of the battle and then the winning of the war. We have managed to take a couple of nicks out of it, a couple of pieces out of it by sticking those repeaters and other bills that the President actually ended up signing. So, you know, we will need some Democratic support in order to get riders out of the Senate and even more Democrats to prevent a veto if that occurs. But look, I don't think that's a good argument for not trying. The wall cold is created, it's created at the pressure in eastern Kentucky and even though I know you're in the western part of the state, it's heading west. And so we're going to give it our best to try to stop this guy. The ultimate solution obviously is a new president of a different persuasion.
There are some who are suggesting that this could be big enough to lead to a government shutdown in the appropriation process. Could it go that far?

No, I don't think so. I mean if you pass individual appropriation bills, you don't have a government-wide shutdown. If the President vetoes a bill that temporarily shuts down the environmental protection agency, I don't think that's a national calamity. It's an argument over what the bill ought to say.

With regard to the final budget process, some have suggested that this would be an opportunity for those who oppose the new provisions of the 2014 Farm Bill to go after farm programs and specifically go after crop insurance. What would be your thoughts on those attacks for farm programs spending and could the USDA's budget be subject to greater cuts?

Well, I'm opposed to unraveling the farm bill for their appropriations process, but I do think it's important to have an appropriation process, you know, the past the individual built, which hasn't been done and certainly in recent memory. as opposed to bawling it all up into one great big omnibus appropriation where, you know, you do have a potential for a government-wide shutdown then. So I think the power of the purse is the best tool we have available. It doesn't guarantee the outcome, but we're going to make an effort across the board to pass each individual appropriation bill that's from the government. That's 12 of them. And we probably have some pretty big arguments over individual appropriation bills that fund different parts of the government over our priorities versus the administration.
Do you see tax reform on the congressional agenda and specifically toward the estate tax or the death tax and then the tax extenders that small business and agriculture are so interested in?

Well, there are three separate issues. They're on the death tax. We had an amendment on the budget week before last, on the death tax, a total repeal of it. It passed. That doesn't get it done, but it certainly indicates the sentiment of the Senate. As you may recall, Jeff, I'm personally responsible for the $5 million per person exemption. that's in car law, which is also indexed for inflation and permanent law. I was able to get that in the 2012 fiscal cliff deal that I negotiated with the Vice President. So that will protect about 99% of Kentucky's farms and small businesses. But I'd like to get rid of the death tax altogether. We had a vote on that during the course of the budget passed. That alone doesn't get rid of it, but it certainly shows where the where the sentiment is, I'd like to get rid of the death tax entirely. The 179 expensive provision, which are part of that typical, what's called the extender package, I'd like to make that permanent, but in the absence of making that permanent, we'll certainly pass an extender package before the year is out. With regard to comprehensive overall tax reform, I don't see how we can do that with President Obama. He has a totally different a set of priorities. He wants to maintain the high rates that he's been able to achieve on individuals and small businesses. We don't think that's a good idea. So I can't imagine that we're going to be able to do system-wide comprehensive tax reform with this president.
